blocks.text: Amides contain the functional group -CONH2. Because they can be made from carboxylic acids they are sometimes called acid amides. They are made by reacting acyl chlorides with ammonia or primary amines at room temperature, releasing white fumes of hydrogen chloride:

items: CH3COCl + NH3 -> CH3CONH2 + HCl (ethanamide); C6H5COCl + NH3 -> C6H5CONH2 + HCl (benzamide).

blocks.alt: CH3-C(=O)-Cl + NH3 gives CH3-C(=O)-NH2 + HCl. Below: benzoyl chloride (ring-C(=O)-Cl) + NH3 gives benzamide (ring-C(=O)-NH2) + HCl.
blocks.caption: Amides from acyl chlorides and ammonia (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 127).

items: CH3COCl + CH3CH2NH2 -> CH3CONHCH2CH3 + HCl (N-ethylethanamide); CH3COCl + C6H5NH2 -> CH3CONHC6H5 + HCl (N-phenylethanamide).

blocks.alt: CH3-C(=O)-Cl (ethanoyl chloride) + CH3-CH2-NH2 gives CH3-C(=O)-NH-CH2-CH3 (N-ethyl ethanamide) + HCl. Below: CH3-C(=O)-Cl + phenyl amine gives CH3-C(=O)-NH-ring (N-phenyl ethanamide) + HCl.
blocks.caption: Amides from acyl chlorides and primary amines (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 127).

items: The HCl formed reacts with another molecule of ammonia or amine to form a salt (NH3 + HCl -> NH4+ Cl-; RNH2 + HCl -> RNH3+ Cl-), so an excess of ammonia or amine is used to complete the reaction.

blocks.alt: R-NH2 + HCl gives R-NH3(+) Cl(-). Below: NH3 + HCl gives NH4(+) Cl(-).
blocks.caption: Salt formation by an amine and by ammonia with HCl (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 128).

blocks.title: Physical properties
blocks.text: All amides except methanamide, a liquid, are solids with sharp melting points, and they have quite high boiling points because of strong hydrogen bonding between molecules. In N-substituted amides the melting and boiling points fall as the number of alkyl substituents increases, because there are fewer N-H hydrogens for hydrogen bonding.

Amides are much weaker bases than aliphatic amines; unlike amines, they form neutral solutions in water. They show resonance: the lone pair on nitrogen is delocalised towards the oxygen of the carbonyl group (R-CO-NH2 <-> R-C(O-)=NH2+), which makes the electrons on nitrogen less available and so decreases the basicity. The partial double-bond character between carbon and nitrogen also makes the amide C-N bond (132 pm) shorter than an ordinary C-N single bond (147 pm).

blocks.alt: R-C(=O)-NH2 with a lone pair on N and two curly arrows (the C=O electrons move onto O; the N lone pair moves into the C-N bond), a double-headed resonance arrow, and R-C(-O-)=NH2+.
blocks.caption: Resonance in an amide (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 128).

blocks.alt: R-C(=O)-NH2 with an arrow to its C-N bond labelled (132 pm), and R-CH2-NH2 with an arrow to its C-N bond labelled (147 pm).
blocks.caption: C-N bond lengths in an amide and in an amine (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 128).

blocks.text: Amides are the least reactive acid derivatives, because the nitrogen lone pair, delocalised over the carbonyl oxygen, reduces the partial positive charge (electrophilic power) of the carbonyl carbon. Their reactions are slow and need prolonged heating or a catalyst (acid or base).

items: Acid hydrolysis gives the carboxylic acid and an ammonium salt: CH3CONH2 + H2O + HCl -> CH3COOH + NH4Cl.
Base-catalysed hydrolysis gives the salt of the acid and ammonia: CH3CONH2 + NaOH -> CH3COONa + NH3; the free acid is obtained with dilute HCl: CH3COONa + HCl -> CH3COOH + NaCl.
Reduction with lithium tetrahydridoaluminate(III) in dry ethoxyethane (ether) gives primary amines: CH3CONH2 + 4[H] -> CH3CH2NH2 + H2O; C6H5CONH2 + 4[H] -> C6H5CH2NH2 + H2O (phenylmethanamine).

blocks.alt: CH3-C(=O)-NH2 + H2O + HCl gives CH3-C(=O)-OH + NH4Cl.
blocks.caption: Acid hydrolysis of ethanamide (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 128).

blocks.alt: CH3-C(=O)-NH2 + NaOH gives CH3-C(=O)-O-Na+ + NH3. Below: CH3-C(=O)-O-Na+ + HCl gives CH3-C(=O)-OH + NaCl.
blocks.caption: Base hydrolysis of ethanamide and acidification of the salt (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 129).

blocks.alt: CH3-C(=O)-NH2 + 4[H], with LiAlH4 over and Dry ether under the arrow, gives CH3-CH2-NH2 + H2O. Below: benzamide (benzene ring-C(=O)-NH2) + 4[H] (LiAlH4, dry ether) gives ring-CH2-NH2 + H2O.
blocks.caption: Reduction of ethanamide and benzamide with LiAlH4 (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 129).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed benzamide reduction draws both rings with only two C=C bonds; they are benzene rings (LiAlH4 reduces only the C=O), as drawn above.
